title: Fanny Mendelssohn's Song and Queen Victoria
text:
Fanny Mendelssohn was born in 1805, four years before her brother Felix. Both were musical prodigies, taught by the same teachers in Berlin. But their father, Abraham, wrote to Fanny in 1820 that music might become Felix's profession, while for her it could only ever be an ornament. A woman of her class was not expected to publish or perform in public.

Fanny kept composing: hundreds of songs and piano pieces, chamber music and choral works. Felix admired her and asked her opinion of his own work. Yet he too discouraged her from publishing. Instead, a few of her songs appeared in his early collections under his own name.

In 1842 Felix visited Queen Victoria and Prince Albert at Buckingham Palace. The queen offered to sing one of his songs and chose "Italien," which she loved. Felix wrote home that he had to confess that the song was actually by his sister. Victoria then sang one of his own, and sang it well.

Fanny married the painter Wilhelm Hensel, who encouraged her, and she hosted famous Sunday concerts at the family home in Berlin. In 1846, at forty, she finally began to publish under her own name. In May 1847 she died suddenly of a stroke while rehearsing. Felix, devastated, died six months later.
lesson: Talent kept hidden by family expectations is a loss to everyone. Encouraging a person to claim her own work is a gift we can give while there is still time.
people: Fanny Mendelssohn Hensel, Felix Mendelssohn, Abraham Mendelssohn, Queen Victoria
source: Felix Mendelssohn, letter to his mother, 19 July 1842; R. Larry Todd, Fanny Hensel: The Other Mendelssohn (2010)
